title: Two-sided completeness and congruence subgroups of completed matrix groups
statement:
Let $A$ be a nonarchimedean normed field, meaning a field with a multiplicative real absolute value satisfying $|a+b|\leq\max(|a|,|b|)$. Let $F=\widehat A$ be its complete normed-field completion with its canonical isometric field inclusion $\iota:A\hookrightarrow F$ [lem-sfb-normed-field-completion]. The extended absolute value on $F$ satisfies the same nonarchimedean inequality. For every integer $n\geq0$, give $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$ the topology induced from the finite product $F^{n\times n}$, and write $\|B\|_{\max}=\max_{i,j}|B_{ij}|$, with maximum $0$ for an empty matrix. This is a Hausdorff topological group. For every real $0<r<1$,
$$U_r=\{I_n+B:\|B\|_{\max}<r\}$$
consists of invertible matrices and is an open subgroup; these subgroups form a basis of identity neighborhoods. For $\|B\|_{\max}<1$, the series $\sum_{m\geq0}(-B)^m$ converges to $(I_n+B)^{-1}$. Every net $(g_i)$ Cauchy for both relative differences $g_i^{-1}g_j$ and $g_ig_j^{-1}$ tending to $I_n$ has entrywise limits $g_i\to a$ and $g_i^{-1}\to b$ in $M_n(F)$, with $ab=ba=I_n$; hence it converges in $\operatorname{GL}_n(F)$. In other words this group is complete for its two-sided uniformity. For $n=0$ these assertions concern the trivial group.

proof.text: Give the matrix space its existing nested Pi norm. The finite ultrametric sum inequality bounds each product entry by the product of the maximum entry norms. This supplies a local NormedRing structure with exactly the existing additive metric and topology. The Pi space is complete and ultrametric. The identity norm is at most one, also for n=0.

source.place: Agent matrix-group argument supporting Proposition 7.1.5, pp. 63–64; Lean proof by T7.

proof.text: For a unit g put q=N(g-I)<1 and d=N(g⁻¹-I). The identity g⁻¹-I=-g⁻¹(g-I) gives d≤N(g⁻¹)q. The ultrametric inequality gives N(g⁻¹)≤max(d,1). If N(g⁻¹)>1 these inequalities imply N(g⁻¹)<N(g⁻¹), a contradiction. Thus N(g⁻¹)≤1 and d≤q. This argument also covers the zero ring of empty matrices.

proof.text: Define U_r by the stated norm inequality on units. The product expansion (I+B)(I+C)-I=B+C+BC, ultrametric addition and submultiplicativity prove product closure when r<1; the previous inverse estimate gives inverse closure. Norm continuity proves openness. The inducing map and a metric ball at I give the neighborhood-basis assertion by choosing 0<r<min(ε,1).

source.place: Agent matrix-group argument supporting Proposition 7.1.5, pp. 63–64; Lean proof by T7.

proof.text: Work with any proper filter f and unit-valued map g. From convergence of g_i⁻¹g_j to I choose product-filter sets P,Q on which its value has distance less than one from I. Fix k∈P. On Q, N(g_j)≤N(g_k)(N(I)+1)<M for a positive M. For any ε>0 the same relative convergence and g_j-g_i=g_i(g_i⁻¹g_j-I) now give additive Cauchyness of the values. Apply the same argument to g⁻¹ using the second relative convergence hypothesis.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-complete-field-cauchy-filter-limit], in its recorded general complete-uniform-space form cauchy_map_iff_exists_tendsto, to the two matrix-valued Cauchy filters. Obtain limits a,b; continuity of multiplication and uniqueness of limits give ab=ba=I. Construct the unit l with value a and inverse b. The inducing units embedding into R×Rᵐᵒᵖ gives convergence to l. Specialize to atTop and compose with coordinate evaluation to obtain every clause for directed nets.

proof.text: For an arbitrary Cauchy filter of the infimum of left and right uniformities, its product lies below both group uniformities. Their defining comap formulas give the two relative convergence hypotheses (swap the coordinates for the right one). Apply the filter-level result just proved. The infimum uniformity induces the original topology since both component uniformities do. This proves CompleteSpace.
